reviews.title: Love the Content, Not the Constant Refreshing
reviews.text:
No complaints about the content. However, the constant app refreshing drives me up a wall. I leave the app open but not active all the time so that I can come back to reading from where I left off. However, most of the time I come back to the app it refreshes and goes back to the home screen. I don't always remember wherw it was I left off. It is like leaving a book on a table and someone constantly removing the bookmark when you're not looking. That is a major jerk thing to do.

I am a software developer by trade. Updating the content or upsating the app itself and keeping the user's place in the app is extremely simple to implement, unless the architecture of the app was very poorly designed. For updating the content, you just need to update the links to the articles in whichever data storage system the app uses. For updating the app itself, you can use a variable which keeps track of where the user is in the app. That way you can restore the user's place in the app when it is restarted after the update. Again, only a really poorly designed app would not be able to do either of those things. You can even put in an app setting option so people can choose to still have their bookmark yanked on them after an update if that's their preference. For the rest of us, stop it.

I would go back to getting the print and digital editions (digital for when the Post Office is not considerate with the delivery of the print edition), but it is quite a lot more for both now, when only a few

reviews.title: *Always* “something went wrong”. And no navigation to home except back-back-back
reviews.text:
I love the Economist and am a very long-time subscriber: this refers specifically to how bad this iPad app is. It is broken is in at least two ways and I hope a one-star review might get the developers to focus, as Lord knows nothing else will.
1. This is very long-standing, but if there is a home button I have never found it. To get from an article back to the front page the only way is back, back, back, or force-quit. This is *crazy*. If I am wrong then developers: make it more obvious than “completely buried”.
2. I get a lot of the Economist newsletters and that tends to be my start-point for interacting with articles. If I use my iPad — and I want to use it for this kind of reading, without fail I get a screen saying “something went wrong. We couldn’t load this story. Please wait a moment a try again”. Well, apparently developers, it’s been untold months and this is me giving up.

reviews.title: Worse then ever
reviews.text: You finally got the message that some readers don’t care about the digital gimmicks that were ruining the experience and added the option to download only the print edition.  However, I have to stare for a very extended time at the loading icon before seeing EVERY SINGLE article.  Also, none of the images download.  I’m amazed that an organization of such brilliant people can be so chronically stupid on the basics of digital experience.  I beg you, fire every decision maker who has touched your digital offering and contract with the first person you run into on the street on your way home.  You’ll be able to stop the exorbitant rate hikes and your readers will get the basic experience they expect.

Another commenter made this same point - basic state preservation is absent so if you don’t finish what you were reading before leaving the app, you’ll be dumped back on the Home Screen and have to navigate all the way back to the article you were reading. If this is a briefing from a few weeks back, this will be a pain. This is basic functionality in a news reading app and I am astonished it’s missing. Nearly £400 a year subscription and you can’t just pick up where you left off? Makes the app much less useful for me. Also, auto downloading new issues would be nice.

reviews.title: Audio plays out of order
reviews.text:
When the audio version of a story is finished, the app SHOULD play the next story in the issue. Indeed, this is what the app used to do. Now, when a story is finished, it starts playing whatever story you were in the middle of the last time you opened the app. So if I’m listening to a story in the United States section, it then jumps to the middle (not even the beginning) of a story in the Britain section. This is because that’s the story I was listening to the last time I used the app. This bug makes it impossible to listen to the articles in order, which is exactly what I want to do. 

I almost exclusively consume the audio version. If this bug isn’t fixed, I will be forced to cancel my subscription.

reviews.title: AI Weekly -or- The Contrarian

AI Weekly -or- The Contrarian

The Economist should change its name to one of the two above titles. 

There is so much AI propaganda, it may take up to 50% of the publication. 

They also seem to consistently take a contrarian approach to anyone that has gained power… not just Trump. 

The publication no longer feels centrist, seems to lean left in some opinions, right in others, and promotes policies that would be ruinous to the human race long term. It has increasingly felt more like propaganda than proper journalism. 

Personally, I will no longer pay for propaganda, but I’ll give two stars for the Espresso reporting on daily news, which actually seems to be lifted and adapted from BBC and Reuters.

reviews.title: Liberal editorial bias, no real economic diversity
reviews.text:
The Economist markets itself as independent and centrist, but the coverage is consistently left-leaning and heavily weighted toward Keynesian economics. There’s little space for alternative perspectives like Austrian economics, supply-side theory, or genuine classical liberal thought. Most issues present progressive policy solutions as the obvious answer and frame skepticism of government intervention as backward.
For a publication that claims to value “free thinking,” it’s remarkably narrow in which economic schools it takes seriously. Austrian economists and their critiques of central banking get dismissed or ignored. Supply-side arguments barely get fair treatment. If you want actual editorial diversity and intellectual rigor from multiple economic perspectives, you won’t find it here.
I’d respect The Economist more if it was honest about its ideological leanings instead of pretending to be the rational, centrist voice. Real independence means genuinely engaging with competing ideas, not just Keynesian orthodoxy.

reviews.title: Needs lots of improvements
reviews.text:
Even if I’ve downloaded an issue, the app still needs Internet access. If I download issues and then go on an airplane and reopen the app, it still needs Internet access to show any articles or play any audio — defeating the entire purpose of downloading the issue for offline access.

The reason appears to be a combination of bad requirements, coding, and testing. It is a bad requirement to require network connectivity to view an issue or play its audio while offline. Poor coding leads to a terrible outcome since the already downloaded data should be presented to the user even when offline. Lastly, it seems that the testers never tested such use cases while offline (airplanes or elevators/lifts or garages/carparks or anywhere else where network access is not available).

I love The Economist’s content. I have also been a user of The Economist app for as long as it has been out, and I continue to be disappointed in its performance.
